scenes.tts: How do you find which compartment holds a protein? Chapter one showed how pumps and leaks help compartments keep distinct chemistries. To relate that chemistry to a protein, first find where the protein sits.
scenes.caption: How do you find which compartment holds a protein? Chapter 1 showed how pumps and leaks help compartments keep distinct chemistries. To relate that chemistry to a protein, first find where the protein sits.
scenes.visual: Open on chapter 1's familiar cell cutaway, with its soft grey outline breathing and RED-ORANGE proton dots drifting. Keep only the lysosome and nucleus labels active; the Golgi, ER and mitochondrion remain as dim, unlabelled context. A GOLD arrow on the lysosome points inward; a dim GOLD mitochondrial arrow points outward. At left, the pH ladder is faint, with its WHITE DASHED cytosol line at 7.2. Keep chapter 1's colour map (protons RED-ORANGE, calcium TEAL, pumps GOLD, leak GREY, cytosol WHITE DASHED). Before narration, show a small MAGENTA star labelled 'protein ?' hovering above the cutaway, clearly outside every compartment, and the white question 'Which compartment holds it?' On 'Chapter one', the two pump arrows pulse. On 'first find', faint MAGENTA dotted arrows point from the star to the lysosome, nucleus and cytosol in turn while the question stays.
scenes.narration: How do you find which compartment holds a protein? Chapter 1 showed how pumps and leaks help compartments keep distinct chemistries. To relate that chemistry to a protein, first find where the protein sits.

scenes.visual: Title 'Follow the Markers' fades in over the top for 2 s, replacing the question. The world keeps moving: dots drift, cell outline breathes, the magenta star bobs.

scenes.tts: A fluorescence image can show a protein at the lysosome. But at is not inside. That image alone cannot tell which side of the membrane it is on.
scenes.caption: A fluorescence image can show a protein at the lysosome. But at is not inside. That image alone cannot tell which side of the membrane it is on.
scenes.visual: Camera pushes in on the lysosome, drawn as a thick grey ring. Magenta stars gather as a glowing patch on the ring (label 'imaging: at the lysosome'). On 'at is not inside', the view splits into two small copies of the ring: left, stars stuck on the outer face (label 'on it'); right, stars floating in the lumen (label 'in it'). Both copies look identical after a soft schematic diffraction blur; a white question mark sits between them.
scenes.narration: A fluorescence image can show a protein at the lysosome. But at is not inside. That image alone cannot tell which side of the membrane it is on.

scenes.tts: So labs also take cells apart. They break cells and separate the pieces by a series of centrifuge spins. Organelles overlap across these crude fractions; no fraction is assumed pure.
scenes.caption: So labs also take cells apart. They break cells and separate the pieces by a series of centrifuge spins. Organelles overlap across these crude fractions; no fraction is assumed pure.
scenes.visual: Pull back: the cell opens and its contents enter one large homogenate tube. The pH ladder slides away. Show a left-to-right sequence of increasingly strong centrifuge spins, passing the supernatant forward after each collection; each collected output transforms into F1, F2, F3 and F4. Do not depict four tubes being centrifuged in parallel. Nucleus-rich material is collected early, lysosome-rich material later and soluble cytosol last, matching the practice profiles. Each collected fraction visibly contains a mixture. The subject fills about 65% of frame height. On 'no fraction', add the white label 'no fraction assumed pure' and the tag 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: So labs also take cells apart. They break cells and separate the pieces by a series of centrifuge spins. Organelles overlap across these crude fractions; no fraction is assumed pure.

scenes.visual: No words: the four collected fractions settle into a row. Each holds a mixture, with nucleus-rich material mostly in F1, lysosome-rich material mostly in F3 and soluble white cytosol haze mostly in F4; other material overlaps without implying that every component occurs in every tube. Tubes sway gently. Tag: 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: To read the fractions, measure markers, proteins whose home is already known. Histone H three marks the nucleus. Cathepsin D marks the lysosome. Pyruvate kinase marks the cytosol. Each marker spreads across the fractions in its own shape.
scenes.caption: To read the fractions, measure markers, proteins whose home is already known. Histone H3 marks the nucleus. Cathepsin D marks the lysosome. Pyruvate kinase marks the cytosol. Each marker spreads across the fractions in its own shape.
scenes.visual: The tubes turn into the x-axis of a bar chart, 'share of protein', F1 to F4. Just before each marker is named, its bars begin growing from the tubes; they settle as the name finishes, and a thin line joins the bar tops: histone H3 (LAVENDER) 0.80, 0.10, 0.05, 0.05; cathepsin D (RED-ORANGE, the acid-lumen colour) 0.05, 0.20, 0.60, 0.15; pyruvate kinase (WHITE) 0.05, 0.05, 0.10, 0.80. Each profile line glows as it is named, then all three stay slightly dimmed. Tag: 'practice numbers from the lesson'. Use a compact three-entry legend mapping the marker colours to nucleus, lysosome and cytosol; do not add a second miniature cell diagram.
scenes.narration: To read the fractions, measure markers, proteins whose home is already known. Histone H3 marks the nucleus. Cathepsin D marks the lysosome. Pyruvate kinase marks the cytosol. Each marker spreads across the fractions in its own shape.

scenes.tts: A protein that stays associated tends to travel with its compartment. So an unknown is assigned provisionally to the marker group whose full profile it most closely shares.
scenes.caption: A protein that stays associated tends to travel with its compartment. So an unknown is assigned provisionally to the marker group whose full profile it most closely shares.
scenes.visual: A MAGENTA profile line labelled 'unknown' slides in above the chart, shaped like a histone-style early peak (schematic, no numbers). On 'full profile', it is laid over each example marker line in turn; against cathepsin D and pyruvate kinase the gaps between the two lines shade grey and large; against histone H3 the two lines nearly coincide and the gap shading almost vanishes. The unknown's line takes a LAVENDER edge and an arrow points to the nucleus label: 'provisional: nuclear'. Tag: 'schematic'. The rule appears across the top in white: 'compare full profiles'.
scenes.narration: A protein that stays associated tends to travel with its compartment. So an unknown is assigned provisionally to the marker group whose full profile it most closely shares.

scenes.tts: In 2016, Georg Borner's group did this with mass spectrometry. They reported localization information for more than eight thousand seven hundred HeLa proteins. Curated markers guided organellar assignments. Proteins split between compartments can yield mixed profiles and uncertain assignments.
scenes.caption: In 2016, Georg Borner's group did this with mass spectrometry. They reported localization information for more than 8,700 HeLa proteins. Curated markers guided organellar assignments. Proteins split between compartments can yield mixed profiles and uncertain assignments.
scenes.visual: The chart shrinks to one small tile at the top left. Behind it, a wall of many tiny localization readouts fills the frame: confident organellar profiles take muted compartment colours, nuclear and cytosolic global-distribution bars use simple neutral shapes, and some readouts stay GREY. A counter rises to '8,710 HeLa proteins', with the separate label 'localization information, 2016'. On 'split between compartments', a handful of blended profiles slide to one side, labelled 'mixed / uncertain'. Tag: 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: In 2016, Georg Borner's group did this with mass spectrometry. They reported localization information for more than 8,700 HeLa proteins. Curated markers guided organellar assignments. Proteins split between compartments can yield mixed profiles and uncertain assignments.

scenes.tts: So a match is provisional. You would want a second marker that agrees, repeated fractionations, and an imaging check in intact cells.
scenes.caption: So a match is provisional. You would want a second marker that agrees, repeated fractionations, and an imaging check in intact cells.
scenes.visual: Back to the single chart with the magenta unknown matched to its marker. A white 'provisional' stamp sits on it. On each item, a checkbox ticks beside the chart: a second lavender marker line drops in and also matches ('second marker'), the tubes briefly refill and the bars redraw almost the same ('repeat'), and a small intact cell lights up the nucleus magenta ('imaging').
scenes.narration: So a match is provisional. You would want a second marker that agrees, repeated fractionations, and an imaging check in intact cells.

scenes.tts: One more test asks whether an enzyme is enclosed by a membrane. In a 1951 report, de Duve's group found acid phosphatase acting less than expected in fresh fractions. More activity appeared once the particles were damaged.
scenes.caption: One more test asks whether an enzyme is enclosed by a membrane. In a 1951 report, de Duve's group found acid phosphatase acting less than expected in fresh fractions. More activity appeared once the particles were damaged.
scenes.visual: Camera returns to the lysosome ring from s02, now as a sealed container in a test tube, drawn large. Inside, a GOLD-outlined enzyme block labelled 'acid phosphatase' (cartoon, not a structure); outside, small GREEN substrate dots that bounce off the grey membrane. Label: '1951: fresh fractions'. A small activity meter beside the tube reads low. On 'particles were damaged', a crack appears in a second container next to it, a few substrate dots slip in, and its meter climbs. Meters are labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: One more test asks whether an enzyme is enclosed by a membrane. In a 1951 report, de Duve's group found acid phosphatase acting less than expected in fresh fractions. More activity appeared once the particles were damaged.

scenes.tts: Picture the enzyme sealed in the lumen, its substrate outside and unable to cross. Now add detergent to open the membranes. What happens to the activity?
scenes.caption: Picture the enzyme sealed in the lumen, its substrate outside and unable to cross. Now add detergent to open the membranes. What happens to the activity?
scenes.visual: The damaged container fades; only the sealed one remains, with green substrate dots bouncing off it. A dropper labelled 'detergent' tilts over the tube but does not release. On 'What happens', the activity meter pulses with a white question mark and two faint arrows, up and down. Question card at top: 'Detergent: activity up or down?'
scenes.narration: Picture the enzyme sealed in the lumen, its substrate outside and unable to cross. Now add detergent to open the membranes. What happens to the activity?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card stays. Substrate dots keep bouncing gently off the membrane; the meter pulses slowly. Nothing opens yet.

scenes.tts: It rises, as long as detergent does not change the enzyme itself. The substrate can now reach it. Activity hidden behind a membrane is called latency.
scenes.caption: It rises, as long as detergent does not change the enzyme itself. The substrate can now reach it. Activity hidden behind a membrane is called latency.
scenes.visual: Just before 'It rises', the dropper releases and the grey membrane begins opening and dispersing into fragments. Green substrate dots stream in to the gold enzyme, and small product dots pop out. The activity meter climbs and holds high. On 'latency', a white label appears: 'latency = membrane-hidden activity'. A small side-by-side miniature shows sealed (meter low) and opened (meter high).
scenes.narration: It rises, as long as detergent does not change the enzyme itself. The substrate can now reach it. Activity hidden behind a membrane is called latency.

scenes.visual: No words: substrate keeps streaming to the gold enzyme, product dots accumulate in the tube, and the activity meter holds high with a gentle flicker. Tag: 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Following these hidden enzymes across fractions led his group to propose the lysosome in 1955. De Duve later shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
scenes.caption: Following these hidden enzymes across fractions led his group to propose the lysosome in 1955. De Duve later shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
scenes.visual: The opened tube shrinks back into the F1 to F4 rack. Several gold enzyme icons with latency meters appear over the rack; their profiles have matching shapes and peak in the same region rather than appearing in one pure fraction. They merge into a single round block that slots back into the rebuilt cell cutaway as the lysosome, label 'lysosome proposed, 1955'.
scenes.narration: Following these hidden enzymes across fractions led his group to propose the lysosome in 1955. De Duve later shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

scenes.tts: The wall that holds a lumen's chemistry also hides what sits inside it. So place the protein first, by its whole profile and independent checks. Then ask what its compartment's chemistry does for it.
scenes.caption: The wall that holds a lumen's chemistry also hides what sits inside it. So place the protein first, by its whole profile and independent checks. Then ask what its compartment's chemistry does for it.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full chapter 1 world: cell cutaway right with a GOLD lysosome pump pointing inward, a GOLD mitochondrial pump pointing outward and drifting RED-ORANGE dots; the pH ladder returns on the left beside a small F1 to F4 profile tile. Clear the example nuclear assignment from s05, then move the MAGENTA star back to its neutral query position above the cutaway with a small '?'; do not place it inside the cytosol. The tile shows only the generic rule 'Whole profile, then confirm' (tag 'schematic'). On 'what its compartment's chemistry does', the lysosome marker on the ladder pulses at 4.7 and the hook question from s00 returns faintly, then fades.
scenes.narration: The wall that holds a lumen's chemistry also hides what sits inside it. So place the protein first, by its whole profile and independent checks. Then ask what its compartment's chemistry does for it.

scenes.line: Place a protein by its whole profile, then confirm it.
scenes.visual: End card in large white text over the dimmed world: 'Place a protein by its whole profile, then confirm it.' Behind it, the profile lines in the tile slowly redraw and the cell keeps breathing.
